name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,770

clue.text: Cross? Violently angry, I will get to snapping bones, possibly

indicators.note: something treated violently is thrown about

blocks.note: a cross is the letter X

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you are cross, and the reply is that they are so furious they will soon be breaking bones.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening question mark makes 'Cross?' look like a question about mood; it is the letter X. 'Snapping' is photographing, not breaking, which the 'possibly' flags.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a pun: 'snap' is slang for taking a photograph, so photographing bones with X-rays is one way of snapping them.

clue.text: Console youngster, shortly covered in kisses

indicators.note: said shortly, a word is cut short, so BOY loses its last letter

blocks.note: X is a kiss; two of them

explanation.surface: An adult comforts a child by smothering them in kisses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Console' reads as a verb, to comfort, in the surface; it is the noun, a games console.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Microsoft's games machine is one kind of console, the box that plugs into a television.

clue.text: Island's unnamed lizard detailed by active conservationists

indicators.note: N is the abbreviation for name

blocks.note: the National Trust, the British heritage and conservation charity
IGUANA without its N and without its final A

explanation.surface: An island's nameless lizard is being described in detail by busy conservation workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'described closely'; read it as de-tailed. 'Unnamed' works the same way, removing N for name.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this Caribbean country, home of St John's, is one of many islands.

clue.text: Characteristic style of Oscar Wilde I am occasionally to cover

indicators.note: something done occasionally happens only now and then, so only every other letter is taken
to cover something is to go over and around it

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of WILDEIAM
Oscar is O in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A remark about Oscar Wilde's distinctive way of writing, as if Wilde were speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar and Wilde go together so naturally that the solver reads them as one name; they are split, Oscar giving O and Wilde starting the letter run.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an idiom can mean the distinctive manner of an artist or school, a characteristic style.

clue.text: Comes through, in adversity - takes balls

blocks.note: in cricket an over is six balls bowled

explanation.surface: Someone survives a bad time, and it takes courage ('balls') to do it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' reads as slang for nerve; here it is the cricket over, six deliveries in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: recovering from an illness or setback is coming through it, and 'in adversity' names the kind of thing overcome.

clue.text: Tell's apple, brief hazard for lad's crown

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so RISK loses its last letter

blocks.note: the top letter of LAD, which RIS replaces

explanation.surface: William Tell shooting an apple off his son's head, a danger to the boy's crown.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the William Tell legend, so 'Tell' looks like a name; it is the verb, and the apple is just letters to edit.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: to apprise is to inform, from the French 'appris', learned, so telling someone news fits.

clue.text: Laid odds (only evens) against increases

indicators.note: evens are the even-numbered positions, so only letters two, four, six and eight are kept

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of LAIDODDS
against = to, as in 'back to the wall'

explanation.surface: A bookmaker offered odds, all at evens, against something happening.
explanation.walkthrough: The betting words 'odds' and 'evens' look like racing talk; 'evens' is the instruction to keep even-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to add to a pile or a problem is to make it bigger, to increase it.

clue.text: Penniless, devout old character rising within

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word rising reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: a rune is a letter of an old alphabet

explanation.surface: A poor, devout figure from long ago who rises up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' reads as a person; it is a letter, the rune.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: penury is poverty, so being penurious means lacking money.

clue.text: Innocent lass, German girl, gets naked on leaving Germany

blocks.note: Inge is a German girl's name
D is the international vehicle code for Germany; it is removed

explanation.surface: An innocent German girl strips once she has left her country.
explanation.walkthrough: D for Germany comes from Deutschland, as on car stickers.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre term: the ingenue is the stock role of an innocent, unworldly young woman.

clue.text: Nosh with setters followed by hanky-panky around southern county

indicators.note: followed by means coming after

blocks.note: nosh and eats are both slang for food
hanky-panky is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: A cosy, racy picture of food, company and flirting in the south of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southern' looks like part of the definition, but it supplies the S inside EATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the county on England's south coast containing Brighton and Hastings is one county among many.

clue.text: Bamboozled and unmasked idiot breaking in

indicators.note: a burglar breaking in gets inside

blocks.note: to be outed is to be exposed

explanation.surface: A fool is caught breaking into a house and has his mask pulled off, baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking in' belongs to the burglary picture, which hides that it is the instruction to put one word inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: being beaten by someone cleverer leaves you bamboozled, fooled.

clue.text: Hot drink with cinnamon, e.g., using only a bit

indicators.note: using only a bit of something means taking a small piece of it, so the answer is a stretch of the letters

explanation.surface: A recipe note: warm drink with cinnamon, just a pinch.
explanation.walkthrough: The recipe surface makes 'only a bit' sound like a quantity of spice; it is telling you the answer is a small part of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: negus, named after Colonel Francis Negus, is warm port or sherry with sugar and spice, a hot drink.

clue.text: Willing for those neglected originally to be represented in series

indicators.note: originally means at the start
re-presented means presented again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A call for neglected groups to get fair representation on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about diversity on screen; 'represented' is the anagram instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the HBO fantasy drama is a television series.

clue.text: On board a cabin cruiser, each passenger heads to topside

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
in a down clue the top side is above

blocks.note: a board is a table, as in 'bed and board'

explanation.surface: Passengers on a cabin cruiser all go up on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' reads as one nautical phrase; split it, and 'On' alone is the definition while 'board' is TABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'that's not on' means it is not acceptable, so 'on' alone means acceptable.

clue.text: It nips, it uses teeth heartlessly, it's more snappy

indicators.note: without a heart means without the middle

blocks.note: a crab nips with its claws
a biter; its middle T goes

explanation.surface: A description of some fierce creature that nips and bites and is getting more irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: Each 'it' starts a new piece; the repetition makes the clue read like one animal being described.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative synonym: crabby means irritable, so crabbier is quicker to snap at people, matching the crab that nips.

clue.text: Girl group first succeeded with brightly-coloured headgear

indicators.note: first means coming before

explanation.surface: A girl group's first hit came wearing colourful headscarves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Girl group' reads as one pop phrase; it splits into the girl and the group, and 'first' puts the group in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plural definition by description: these patterned cotton scarves are knotted round the head, so they count as headgear.

clue.text: They wear shorts and pants

blocks.note: boxer shorts, a style of men's underpants

explanation.surface: A plain statement that some people wear shorts and pants.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English pants are underpants. The clue reads as one list of clothes, but it holds two separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: fighters in the ring wear shorts, and boxer shorts are a loose style of underpants, called pants in Britain.

clue.text: Fault in bit of cinematography rectified - version ready for release

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here its first letter
something rectified is put right, so the letters are set in a new, correct order

explanation.surface: A flaw in some camera work is fixed so the film can go out.
explanation.walkthrough: The film-making surface fits the answer exactly, so the definition hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A film-industry term: the last edit a director approves is the one sent out to cinemas, the version ready for release.

clue.text: Ultimately lose knight to chess champ's closing moves

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end

blocks.note: N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A chess champion loses a knight in the endgame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' just joins the pieces in order. The chess surface is apt: the ending is the last phase of a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A chess term: the last phase of a game, when few pieces remain, is called the ending or endgame.

clue.text: Conned king for power, medal and lordly title

blocks.note: K is the king, as in chess
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: A king was tricked into swapping power for honours and titles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King for power' reads as a trade; it is the instruction to put K where P was.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the rank held by a duke, the highest hereditary title below prince, is a lordly title.

clue.text: Rapidly recruiting US taxmen for high-level domain?

explanation.surface: A US tax agency hurriedly hiring for a senior post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-level' sounds like seniority in a job; the question mark flags that it means literally high up in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition by description: the sky above a country is territory it controls, a domain that is literally high up.

clue.text: Yankee President cycling over to NATO, say

indicators.note: a cycle goes round and round, so letters move from the front round to the back

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An American president turns up at a NATO meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two letters of YMACRON go round to the end. 'Yankee President' reads as one American; they are two pieces, and the president is French.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: NATO is built from the initials of North Atlantic Treaty Organization and spoken as a word.

clue.text: Rabble-rousing leader has women's group round the twist

indicators.note: a leader goes at the front
to have something is to hold it

blocks.note: the Women's Institute, a British community organisation for women

explanation.surface: A demagogue brings a women's group to the brink of madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round the twist' is British slang for crazy, so the phrase reads as one idea; 'the' is letters and 'twist' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: squirming about in pain means twisting the body.

clue.text: Try to pot one red, initially maintaining break, finally switching to the rest

indicators.note: initially means at the start

blocks.note: in snooker, to take a ball is to pot it
its final K is replaced by THE

explanation.surface: A snooker player lines up a red and builds a break, then reaches for the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Snooker words are everywhere: break, red, pot and the rest (a cue support). 'The' supplies letters for the swap, and 'rest' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: stopping briefly to recover your breath means resting, as a snooker player might between frames.

clue.text: Drinks cuppa, left unfinished in hurry

indicators.note: something left unfinished lacks its end

blocks.note: to have a drink is to drink it
a cuppa is a cup of tea; its A is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone gulps a cup of tea and leaves it half drunk in a rush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the direction L; with 'unfinished' it means the tea is left incomplete.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: excess speed, the rush of someone late, is hurry; 'in haste' and 'in a hurry' match.

clue.text: I think it's a book

blocks.note: a phrase meaning 'in my view', written as two short words

explanation.surface: Someone guessing what an object is: a book, they think.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I think' reads as hedging; run together, 'to me' (as in 'to me, it's a book') gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: 'to me' means in my opinion, and closed up it is a large heavy volume, a kind of book.

clue.text: Hunter maybe returning horned ibex hides

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the hidden letters read backwards
to hide something is to conceal it, so the answer is concealed in the words

explanation.surface: A hunter coming back with the skin of a horned mountain goat.
explanation.walkthrough: The hunting scene makes 'Hunter' a job; it is a first name, and 'hides' is a verb, not animal skins.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Hunter is the first name of Joe Biden's son, so a Biden is what Hunter is.

clue.text: Fat monk loves eats

blocks.note: Friar Tuck, the stout friar of the Robin Hood stories

explanation.surface: A greedy monk adores his food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eats' looks like a noun (food), the thing the monk loves; it is the verb and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to tuck into a meal is to eat it with gusto.

clue.text: Scattered SAS men finally strike as one

indicators.note: things scattered are strewn about, so the letters land in a new order

explanation.surface: Special forces soldiers, spread out, attack together.
explanation.walkthrough: The SAS is the British Army's special forces regiment. 'Strike' reads as the attack; only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase used in English: 'in a mass', all together, so acting as one body.

clue.text: The Queen Mother entered hot springs

blocks.note: the word itself, opened up to take the others

explanation.surface: The Queen Mother bathing in hot springs.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal title reads as one person, the late Queen Mother; the three words work separately. ER for a queen dates from Elizabeth II's reign.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin plural: Roman public baths fed by warm water were thermae, from the Greek for heat, hence hot springs.
